query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys, the retention of toughness under demanding conditions is governed by the suppression of deleterious nanosegregation of specific solute elements (e.g., Ni, Cr, and Mn) at grain boundaries. Preventing or redirecting this segregation preserves grain-boundary cohesion and thereby maintains ductility and overall toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase high-entropy alloy (for example, a CrMnFeCoNi-type alloy) with a seemingly homogeneous distribution of principal elements across grains and grain boundaries.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled grain-boundary segregation engineering strategy by adding a minor amount of a secondary element (or inducing preexisting secondary phases) that preferentially attracts embrittling solutes away from the grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Perform uniaxial tensile tests at intermediate to elevated temperatures (e.g., 300–700 K) under controlled atmospheres to minimize oxidation, ensuring that any toughness loss is primarily due to solute mobility and not extraneous environmental effects.
generation.structural_mediator: The local chemical composition at grain boundaries (including any preformed secondary phases or segregation modifiers) which modulates intergranular cohesion.
generation.mechanism: At service temperatures, increased atomic mobility can drive nanoclustering of elements such as Ni, Cr, and Mn at grain boundaries, reducing intergranular cohesion and promoting crack initiation. By adding a controlled secondary element or phase that sequesters these embrittling solutes, the local grain-boundary chemistry is modified, thus mitigating decohesion and allowing sustained toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy that exhibits marked intergranular cracking and reduced ductility at elevated temperatures, the engineered alloy will show higher toughness and ductility. Microstructural analyses (e.g., atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM) should reveal diminished or redirected nanosegregation at grain boundaries.
generation.baseline: High-entropy alloys without grain-boundary engineering, which under thermal activation show pronounced nanoclustering at grain boundaries leading to intergranular fracture and toughness loss.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for single-phase or near-single-phase high-entropy alloys with predominantly fcc structures and in temperature ranges where solute mobility is significant but oxidation effects are minimized. It is most directly applicable to alloys in which embrittlement is known to be linked to localized grain-boundary segregation.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal concentration and choice of the secondary element (or phase) necessary to effectively capture the embrittling solutes without adversely affecting other properties is not yet determined. Additionally, the temperature window over which segregation is most critical may vary with alloy design.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of a high-entropy alloy (e.g., CrMnFeCoNi): one set as the baseline and the other with a minor addition of a grain-boundary modifying element intended to form secondary phases that attract Ni/Cr/Mn. Conduct identical high-temperature tensile tests and in situ microstructural characterizations.
measurements: Tensile yield strength, ductility, and fracture toughness at elevated temperatures
Atom probe tomography or high-resolution TEM analysis of grain-boundary composition
Fractography to evaluate the mode (intergranular vs. transgranular) of fracture
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in toughness (i.e., higher ductility and delayed onset of intergranular cracking) relative to the baseline, or if microstructural characterization shows similar levels of nanosegregation at grain boundaries in both cases, then the hypothesis that grain-boundary segregation control governs toughness retention would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs reduces GB cohesion in single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys. AbstractThe loss of ductility with temperature has been widely observed in tensile tests of single-phase face-centered cubic structured high-entropy alloys (HEAs). However, the fundamental mechanism for such a ductility loss remains unknown. Here, we show that ductility loss in the CrMnFeCoNi HEA upon deformation at intermediate temperatures is correlated with cracking at grain boundaries (GBs). Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs, as detected by atom probe tomography, reduces GB cohesion and promotes crack initiation along GBs. We further demonstrated a GB segregation engineering strategy to avoid ductility loss by shifting the fast segregation of principal elements from GBs into preexisting Cr-rich secondary phases. We believe that GB decohesion by nanoclustering multiprincipal elements is a common phenomenon in HEAs. This study not only provides insights into understanding ductility loss but also offers a strategy for tailoring ductility-temperature relations in HEAs.

We revealed the key mechanism responsible for the loss of the ductility with increasing temperature, a phenomenon widely reported in the single-phase fcc HEAs that are composed of three or more elements of Al, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, and Ni. SEM of tensioned sample surfaces of single-phase coarse-grained Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA (grain size around 50 μm) suggested that ductility loss is correlated with the intergranular cracking. However, TEM along GBs confirmed that there are no precipitates of secondary phases along GBs. On the basis of APT analysis, we explored that ductility loss is attributed to fast nanosegregation of principal elements Ni, Cr, and Mn separately into GBs, which reduce GB cohesion and promote crack initiation along GBs. We further demonstrated a GB segregation engineering strategy to evade ductility loss by migrating fast segregation of the principal elements from GBs into preexisting Cr-rich secondary phases in an example HEA, i.e., Cr26Mn20Fe20Co20Ni14. Our work not only provides insights into understanding ductility loss but also offers a GB segregation engineering strategy of tailoring strength-ductility-temperature relations in HEAs.
